questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a shared resource collapses
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an open-access resource degrades
questions.stem: A fishing ground open to all boats has seen catches fall sharply; what explains the collapse?

options.text: Boats lack modern navigation tools and miss the best grounds
options.misconception: blames missing technology rather than open access incentives

options.text: Government quotas were set too high for every season
options.misconception: assumes a quota existed when the ground is open access

options.text: Each fisher gains full benefit but shares the cost of depletion
Fish populations naturally cycle and will rebound next year
options.misconception: treats overfishing collapse as a harmless natural cycle

questions.explanation: Open access rewards individual harvest while spreading depletion costs across all users, so stocks collapse. Technology or natural cycles do not explain the systematic decline.
questions.hint: Think about who keeps the benefit and who bears the loss.

questions.topic: Sustainable offtake from a regenerating resource
questions.stem: A forest regrows 120 cubic metres of timber per year; what is the maximum sustainable annual harvest in cubic metres?
questions.explanation: Sustainable offtake equals regeneration, so harvesting 120 cubic metres per year keeps stock constant. Harvesting more depletes the capital stock.
questions.hint: Match harvest to yearly regrowth.

questions.topic: Carrying capacity of a resource
questions.learningObjective: Define carrying capacity in a resource context
questions.stem: In a workplace report on a shared pasture, define carrying capacity and why exceeding it matters.

answer.exemplar: Carrying capacity is the largest population or use level a resource can sustain without degradation; exceeding it erodes the resource base and lowers future yields for all users.

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity sets the upper sustainable use level. Crossing it damages the resource and reduces long-term productivity for everyone dependent on it.
questions.hint: State the sustainable maximum and its consequence.

questions.stem: What is the main weakness of the claim in the report?

options.text: It ignores how technology and institutions shape human outcomes
options.misconception: focuses on climate data gaps rather than the theory's flaw

options.text: It uses too few climate variables to classify regions
options.misconception: treats the problem as incomplete data rather than bad theory

options.text: It treats environmental factors as sole determinants of culture
It confuses weather with long-term climate averages
options.misconception: mistakes the issue for a measurement confusion

questions.explanation: Environmental determinism overstates nature's control and ignores human agency, technology, and institutions. The flaw is causal overreach, not missing data.

questions.stem: An unregulated aquifer is being pumped dry; what drives the depletion?

options.text: Farmers lack drilling technology
options.misconception: blames technology gaps rather than incentives

options.text: Each pumper keeps full benefit while costs are shared
Rainfall recharge is zero everywhere
options.misconception: overstates the recharge problem

options.text: The aquifer is naturally small
options.misconception: attributes depletion to size, not use

questions.explanation: Open access rewards individual pumping while spreading depletion costs, so the aquifer declines. Technology or size are not the root cause.
questions.hint: Who gains and who pays for one more well?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sustainable offtake from a regenerating resource
questions.stem: A grassland regrows 90 tonnes of biomass per year; what is the maximum sustainable annual offtake in tonnes?
questions.explanation: Sustainable offtake equals regeneration at 90 tonnes per year, keeping biomass stock stable. Higher offtake depletes the stock.
questions.hint: Match offtake to yearly regrowth.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Carrying capacity of a resource
questions.stem: Define carrying capacity for a shared resource in one or two sentences.

answer.exemplar: Carrying capacity is the maximum use or population level a resource can sustain indefinitely without degradation; exceeding it reduces future productivity and can collapse the resource.

questions.explanation: Carrying capacity sets the sustainable upper limit. Crossing it degrades the resource and lowers long-term yields.
questions.hint: State the sustainable maximum and its consequence.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Environmental determinism
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects environmental determinism?

options.text: Climate and terrain alone shape a society's culture and economy
Humans adapt environments through technology and institutions
options.misconception: describes possibilism, the opposite view

options.text: Geography sets limits but culture decides outcomes
options.misconception: describes a moderate interactionist view

options.text: Every region develops identical institutions
options.misconception: makes an implausible universal claim

questions.explanation: Environmental determinism holds that the physical environment dictates human outcomes. Possibilism and interactionism allow human agency.
questions.hint: Which view makes nature the sole driver?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why climate zones do not have sharp edges
questions.stem: Why do climate zone maps show transition bands rather than sharp lines?

answer.exemplar: Temperature, rainfall, and seasonality change continuously across latitude and altitude, so boundaries are ecotones where conditions blend rather than abrupt lines.

questions.explanation: Climate variables vary continuously in space, producing transition zones. Sharp lines are cartographic simplifications.
questions.hint: How do climate variables change in space?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability
questions.stem: Living on a fault line is best described as which risk component?

options.text: Hazard, because the earthquake is the threat
options.misconception: confuses the event with the people's location

options.text: Exposure, because residents are in the hazard zone
Vulnerability, because buildings may collapse
options.misconception: confuses structural susceptibility with location

options.text: Resilience, because people can evacuate
options.misconception: mistakes coping capacity for being at risk

questions.explanation: Exposure means being located where a hazard can strike. Vulnerability concerns susceptibility; resilience concerns coping capacity.
questions.hint: Which component is about location in the zone?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The vulnerable share of an exposed population
questions.stem: Of 10000 people exposed to a storm, 2500 are highly vulnerable; what percentage is highly vulnerable?
questions.explanation: 2500 divided by 10000 equals 0.25, or 25 percent. This is the vulnerable share of the exposed population.
questions.hint: Divide vulnerable by exposed, times 100.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Adaptation and mitigation
questions.stem: Switching a bus fleet to electric vehicles is best classified as what?

options.text: Mitigation, because it cuts emissions
Adaptation, because it reduces heat
options.misconception: confuses emission reduction with impact reduction

options.text: Both, because fleets affect climate and heat
options.misconception: conflates the two distinct strategies

options.text: Neither, because buses are public transport
options.misconception: dismisses a real emission-cutting measure

questions.explanation: Electrifying the fleet reduces greenhouse-gas emissions, which is mitigation. It does not directly reduce climate impacts.
questions.hint: Does the action reduce causes or effects?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A barrier against ten years of flood damage
questions.stem: A levee designed for a 10-year flood is exceeded in two consecutive years; what does this show?

options.text: The design was definitely miscalculated
options.misconception: assumes exceedance proves design error

options.text: Consecutive exceedances are possible under probability
Floods now occur on a fixed schedule
options.misconception: assumes periodicity in random events

options.text: The levee protects only ten percent of area
options.misconception: confuses probability with spatial coverage

questions.explanation: A 10-year flood has a 10 percent annual chance, so consecutive exceedances, while unlikely, are possible. This does not prove design error.
questions.hint: What does annual probability allow?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Two totals, opposite per-capita figures
questions.stem: Why can a country have huge total emissions but low per-capita emissions?

answer.exemplar: A large population spreads total emissions across many people, so per-capita figures fall even when the national total is high; the two metrics answer different questions.

questions.explanation: Per-capita divides by population, so large populations lower the per-person figure. Total and per-capita measure different things.
questions.hint: How does population affect the per-person figure?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Per-capita release for one country
questions.stem: A country emits 150 million tonnes of carbon dioxide with 30 million people; what is per-capita release in tonnes?
questions.explanation: 150 million divided by 30 million equals 5 tonnes per person. Per-capita release scales total emissions by population.
questions.hint: Divide total by population.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Comparing two per-capita figures
questions.stem: Country R emits 10 tonnes per person and Country S emits 5 tonnes per person; which statement is correct?

options.text: R's per-capita release is double S's
R's per-capita release is five tonnes more in ratio
options.misconception: confuses absolute difference with ratio

options.text: S's per-capita release is double R's
options.misconception: inverts the ratio

options.text: The two are equal on a per-capita basis
options.misconception: ignores the numerical difference

questions.explanation: 10 divided by 5 equals 2, so R's per-capita release is double S's. The absolute difference is 5 tonnes, not a doubling.
questions.hint: Divide R by S.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Classifying regions by definition
questions.stem: A region defined by a shared economic activity, such as dairy farming, is what type?

options.text: Formal region, because the activity is uniform
Functional region, because farms trade goods
options.misconception: confuses uniform activity with a nodal flow

options.text: Vernacular region, because farmers name it
options.misconception: confuses objective activity with perceived identity

options.text: Transition zone, because farming varies
options.misconception: mistakes a uniform activity area for a boundary

questions.explanation: A formal region has uniform traits or activities throughout. Functional regions centre on nodes, and vernacular regions rest on perception.
questions.hint: Which type requires uniformity?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A region named only by its residents
questions.stem: Why does a vernacular region have fuzzy boundaries?

answer.exemplar: It exists in residents' perception and naming rather than in objective criteria, so different people draw its edges differently and no official boundary fixes them.

questions.explanation: Vernacular regions rest on perception, not objective traits, so their boundaries vary by individual and lack official fixity.
questions.hint: What defines the region's edges?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: One city block, two different sites
questions.stem: A shop's success depends more on foot traffic from a nearby station than on its floor area; which factor is situation?

options.text: Floor area, because it is a physical trait
options.misconception: confuses physical size with relative location

options.text: Foot traffic from the station, because it is relative location
Both, because site and situation merge
options.misconception: collapses two distinct concepts

options.text: Neither, because success is random
options.misconception: denies geographic influence

questions.explanation: Situation is relative location and connections, such as foot traffic from a station. Floor area is a physical site trait.
questions.hint: Which factor is about relative position?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A ridge that silts up and a route that moves
questions.stem: A river port is losing trade because sediment blocks large vessels; what is the geographic response?

options.text: Trade shifts to a deeper, accessible port
Vessels adapt by becoming smaller permanently
options.misconception: assumes fleets shrink rather than reroute

options.text: The port dredges once and never changes
options.misconception: ignores ongoing siltation and cost

options.text: Trade stops entirely worldwide
options.misconception: overstates the local effect globally

questions.explanation: When a port becomes inaccessible, trade flows move to viable alternatives. Fleets do not permanently shrink and trade does not stop globally.
questions.hint: Where does trade go when access is lost?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A common pasture with a new road through it
questions.stem: Why does a new road through a common pasture threaten its sustainability?

answer.exemplar: The road lowers access costs, drawing more users and raising grazing pressure until vegetation degrades and the pasture's long-term productivity falls for everyone.

questions.explanation: Easier access increases use intensity on a shared resource, accelerating degradation. Sustainability requires limiting use.
questions.hint: How does access change use pressure?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why mitigation and adaptation are not substitutes
questions.stem: A policy funds only seawalls and no emission cuts; what risk remains?

options.text: Warming continues, so future impacts worsen beyond wall design
Seawalls eliminate all future flood risk
options.misconception: assumes protection removes the hazard

options.text: Emissions become irrelevant to coastal cities
options.misconception: denies the driver's ongoing role

options.text: Adaptation becomes unnecessary
options.misconception: reverses the actual relationship

questions.explanation: Without mitigation, warming intensifies and can exceed adaptation design limits. Protection alone does not stop the underlying driver.
questions.hint: What happens to impacts if warming continues?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why the top-down map is misleading
questions.stem: A world map shades countries by GDP per capita; what is a key limitation?

options.text: It hides inequality within each country
It shows only historical GDP
options.misconception: assumes the data are outdated

options.text: It exaggerates small countries' area
options.misconception: confuses colour shading with map projection

options.text: It counts only urban GDP
options.misconception: invents a restriction not in the map

questions.explanation: National averages conceal internal variation, so local poverty or wealth pockets disappear. The limitation is aggregation, not age or projection.
questions.hint: What detail is lost in country averages?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why protection alone fails
questions.stem: Why might a higher flood wall increase long-term risk?

answer.exemplar: A higher wall encourages development in the protected zone, raising exposure and potential losses; when the wall is eventually overtopped, damage is greater than if the area had stayed undeveloped.

questions.explanation: Protection can increase exposure by encouraging risky development. Combined with a worsening hazard, eventual failure causes larger losses.
questions.hint: How does protection change development behaviour?
